usedHookFrames: good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch01: A service-ticket printout can expose a fake strategy faster than a polished growth deck.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch02: The strongest player in the room may be weak the moment the game changes shape.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch03: The most dangerous plan in the room may be the one with the cleanest verbs.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch04: A room can agree quickly because nothing costly has been named yet.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch05: Three linked sentences can do more strategic work than a hundred approved initiatives.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch06: Taproom invoices reveal whether an advantage is durable or only lucky once.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch07: One injury log can turn a safety campaign from scattered concern into applied force.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch08: Near targets keep a team moving when the far target is still fog.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch09: Sterile trays fail at the handoff, no matter how clean the rest of the room looks.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch10: Fit is visible when one choice makes the next choice stronger.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch11: Focus begins when a capable team lets some good work stay unfunded.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch12: Growth can widen the very crack that focus was holding closed.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch13: Moving parts create openings a still snapshot cannot show.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch14: Drift can look like character failure until the system is opened.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch15: Integration turns scattered good ideas into one hard-to-copy response.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch16: Claims become strategy only when pressure can test them.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch17: Pressure makes the easiest story feel like judgment.
usedCounterFrames: good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch01: Boldness gets too much credit. A louder goal can hide the missing work: naming the obstacle, choosing what loses protection, and making the actions fit that diagnosis.

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch02: Power is often hiding where the obvious contest stops mattering. Size, money, and rank can lose force when a weaker player changes terms, uses a network, or makes response costly.

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch03: Bad strategy rarely announces itself as confusion. It often arrives as confident language, crowded priorities, and inspiring goals that protect the missing diagnosis from inspection.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch04: Bad strategy persists because vague agreement is useful. It lets groups feel united, protects favored work, and postpones the moment when somebody must lose.

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch05: Treating the kernel as a worksheet breaks it. Diagnosis, guiding policy, and coherent action have to stay connected, or each part becomes another way to avoid choosing.

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch06: Possession gets mistaken for power too easily. An advantage becomes strategic only when it recurs, reinforces itself, and changes the contest more than a copied surface move can.

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch07: Intensity spread everywhere can feel responsible while wasting the point of leverage. Force has to land where the situation bends, even when other problems remain worthy.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch08: Small targets can still be evasions. A proximate objective is the next credible aim that concentrates action while uncertainty still hides the whole route.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch09: Average strength can fool a system owner. In a chain-link system, one indispensable weak step can cap the whole result while stronger steps merely wait behind it.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch10: Design in strategy is arrangement, not polish. The work is to make choices fit together so each one reinforces the response to structural limits.

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch11: Saying fewer words is the shallow version of focus. Strategic focus is selective intensity: choosing where scarce effort concentrates and where respectable work waits.

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch12: Expansion deserves suspicion when it consumes the resource that created strength. Good growth preserves strategic fit; bad growth enlarges scope while dissolving force.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch13: Speed can make a team miss the turn. Dynamics asks what changes next, who reacts, and which later option becomes possible before the first move is chosen.

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch14: Blame feels decisive, but resistance often lives in paths, screens, schedules, and handoffs. Inertia and entropy have to be diagnosed as design problems before effort can matter.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch15: A summary can sound complete while leaving the work unjoined. Strategy comes together when diagnosis, force, timing, structure, and action make each other stronger.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch16: Rigor does not come from a formula. It comes from making the causal claim explicit enough that evidence, challenge, and consequence can improve it.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch17: Confidence can be the trap. Disciplined thinking slows the first explanation long enough to test analogies, preferred evidence, and comfortable stories.
usedTryThisNowFrames: good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch01: Take one active plan and write three lines: the obstacle, the chosen response, and one action you would cut because it does not serve either one.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch02: Pick one fight you are entering today. Write the opponent’s preferred terms, then write one way to change the contest so your own strength matters more.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch03: Open one current plan and underline every action verb. If the verbs do not point to one named obstacle, write “missing diagnosis” in the margin.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch04: Take one recent consensus decision and write the choice it avoided. Name the group or project that would have lost if the plan had been precise.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch05: Write one sentence for diagnosis, one for guiding policy, and one for action. If the third sentence could fit a different diagnosis, rewrite it.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch06: List one advantage you claim. Beside it, write whether it repeats, compounds, or makes matching you costly. Cross out any answer that only worked once.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch07: Circle the one point where effort would change the most downstream outcomes. Write one action that lands there and one tempting action you will leave alone.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch08: Name one uncertainty you cannot resolve yet. Then write the nearest objective that would make tomorrow’s action clearer without pretending to solve the whole path.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch09: Choose one process and mark every indispensable step. Put a star beside the weakest necessary link, then name one repair that changes that link first.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch10: Pick three choices in one plan. Draw arrows between them only where one strengthens another. Any choice with no arrow needs a defense or a cut.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch11: Choose one plan with too many priorities. Mark two efforts as primary, two as secondary, and one as intentionally unfunded for now.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch12: Take one growth option and write the capability it would consume first. If that capability is what makes the strategy work, slow the expansion.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch13: Take one active decision and write the next three likely reactions in order. Circle the move that improves the second or third step, not just the first.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch14: Choose one recurring failure and name the artifact that keeps it alive: a screen, schedule, rule, queue, or handoff. Mark one redesign move beside it.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch15: Pick one decision and draw four boxes: diagnosis, guiding policy, first action, reinforcing action. Cross out any box that does not support the others.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch16: Write one strategy claim as because, therefore, unless. Add one piece of evidence that would force you to revise it.
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch17: Take one decision and write: the story I want to be true, the analogy I am using, and the fact that would make both weaker.
usedQuizExplanationFrames: good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch01:q01: A regional gym chain has a plan that lists new classes, a referral drive, lobby paint, instructor training, and a pricing test. Cancellations are rising because evening classes start late. Which response best fits good strategy?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch01:q02: A college dining service blames low satisfaction on weak marketing, but comment cards show students leave when the allergen station runs out by noon. What should the director do first?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch01:q03: A repair shop owner wants to respond to slipping margins by buying ads, adding Saturday hours, and launching a loyalty card. The parts shelf shows the same three components are always missing. What is the soundest move?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch01:q04: A nonprofit board approves a plan with ten priorities after a quiet retreat. The only hard data says donor renewals drop after delayed thank-you calls. What should a new director challenge?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch01:q05: A city parks team says its strategy is to increase usage, modernize facilities, improve inclusion, build partnerships, and upgrade signage. Weekend field permits are the only service with a waitlist. What is the best critique?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch01:q06: A medical device startup says it will win through bold culture, fast hiring, international expansion, and constant customer listening. Lab notes show sterilization failures are delaying every pilot. Which option shows coherent action?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch01:q07: A school principal inherits a plan full of slogans about excellence and belonging. Attendance records show ninth graders miss the first period after late bus arrivals. What would make the plan strategic?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch01:q08: A bakery cuts its wholesale line after seeing that retail customers spend more per order. Two months later, staff have fewer shifts and retail still misses daily targets because morning production is late. How should you evaluate the cut?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch01:q09: A software team has three proposals after churn rises: add onboarding videos, discount annual plans, and hire customer success reps. Exit interviews show customers leave after one broken data import. What should guide the choice?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch02:q01: A small soccer club keeps losing to richer clubs that recruit faster players. Its coach notices the home field is narrow and rewards set pieces. What response shows hidden power?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch02:q02: A local grocer cannot match a national chain’s prices, but it knows apartment managers who need predictable weekly deliveries. Which action best discovers power?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch02:q03: A university lab competes for grants against famous institutions. It owns a rare microscope with open weekend capacity. What should guide its proposal?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch02:q04: A regional courier is losing urban accounts to a larger rival. Its route data show it reaches remote clinics twice as reliably during storms. What is the strategic implication?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch02:q05: A cybersecurity firm cannot outstaff a major competitor, but its tool updates rules within minutes because engineers sit beside analysts. Which choice uses that power?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch02:q06: A café near a train station cannot beat chains on brand recognition. It can serve commuters in three minutes because the kitchen is beside the pickup window. What would be a weak imitation?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch02:q07: A public school debate team always loses to private schools with more coaches. It notices judges reward evidence packets that arrive before rounds. What should it do?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch02:q08: A startup says it has discovered power because a launch stunt went viral once. Three months later competitors copy the stunt. How should you evaluate the claim?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch02:q09: A regional bank wants to beat national banks on mobile features. Its strongest asset is a loan officer network trusted by local contractors. What question should come first?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch03:q01: A nonprofit plan promises awareness, partnerships, youth engagement, digital reach, and policy change. It never says why donations have fallen. What is the clearest sign of bad strategy?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch03:q02: A school improvement plan says every student will thrive, every teacher will innovate, and every family will feel heard. Attendance data show ninth-grade absences drive most failures. What should happen first?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch03:q03: A product leader presents ten feature launches as the strategy for reducing churn. Support tickets show customers leave after failed data imports. Which critique is strongest?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch03:q04: A city agency calls its plan “A Cleaner, Safer, Smarter Downtown” and funds murals, patrols, bins, cameras, and events. Complaint logs show trash pickup fails after weekend festivals. What action best exposes bad strategy?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch03:q05: A hospital service line misses targets, and leaders respond with a culture campaign, a patient app, a referral lunch, and new posters. Nurse notes show delays start at one intake desk. What pattern is visible?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch03:q06: A museum team votes to keep all twelve membership initiatives because each one has a passionate sponsor. Renewal calls point to one missing evening-access option. What should a strategist do?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch03:q07: A startup says its strategy is “win enterprise,” then lists security, onboarding, integrations, brand, conferences, and hiring. Sales losses trace to one procurement security question. What does the phrase “win enterprise” lack?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch03:q08: A regional airline cuts snacks, lounge access, and customer service hours after losses. It calls the cuts a strategy. Customer data show losses come from unreliable early flights. How should you evaluate the claim?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch03:q09: A department head avoids choosing between two projects by approving both and calling the result a portfolio strategy. Both require the same specialist. What question should a colleague ask?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch04:q01: A committee approves a plan quickly because every department sees its favorite project included. No budget increase is available. What should you infer?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch04:q02: A city task force writes “safe, vibrant, inclusive streets” into its plan. Crash records show one dangerous intersection creates most injuries. What is the most strategic next move?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch04:q03: A family business retreat protects every owner’s pet project because nobody wants a fight. A failing assembly step is causing returns. What does the retreat reward?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch04:q04: A university committee loves the phrase “distinctive pathways,” but enrollment data show two tracks compete for the same faculty. What question should break the fog?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch04:q05: A hospital plan wins approval because every service line is praised equally. Bed data show one service must get priority to reduce waits. What is wrong with the approval?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch04:q06: An arts board gives high scores to proposals that mention access, innovation, community, and experimentation. Canceled productions show cash timing is the recurring failure. What should change?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch04:q07: A software offsite ends with all teams keeping their top priorities, even though one dependency blocks the release. What does this reveal?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch04:q08: A director says vague language is necessary because the organization needs unity. When is that unity counterfeit?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch04:q09: A nonprofit avoids choosing between legal aid and rent relief by calling both “housing stability pillars.” Funding covers only one pilot. What should a strategist do?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch05:q01: A clinic says it will reduce missed visits with reminder texts, stricter fees, and posters. The bus schedule shows patients arrive after the first appointment block. Which answer best uses the kernel?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch05:q02: A distributor entering a new region has strong demand but weak return handling. Which guiding policy fits the diagnosis?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch05:q03: A college tries to improve apprenticeship placement with resume workshops. Employer calls show supervisors are confused by three different college contacts. What coherent action follows?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch05:q04: A startup says its policy is “serve the mid-market,” but its trial data show finance teams activate fastest after one demo type. What is missing?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch05:q05: A theater wants subscription growth and plans a prettier brochure. Seat maps and donor records show older patrons still donate but skip weeknight shows. Which kernel is strongest?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch05:q06: A storm office counts sandbags weekly, but field teams lose contact after roads close. What is the most coherent response?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch05:q07: A manager writes a sharp diagnosis and then lists actions that could belong to almost any problem. What link in the kernel is weak?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch05:q08: A team has three tidy sentences: “Customers are confused. We will simplify. We will update the website.” User tests show confusion happens only during billing calls. How should you evaluate it?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch05:q09: A nonprofit diagnoses volunteer churn, chooses “better engagement,” and schedules a gala. Exit notes say volunteers leave after unclear first shifts. What should change?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch06:q01: A bakery says its advantage is a viral pastry photo from last month. Competitors have already copied the design. What question best tests whether this is a source of power?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch06:q02: An urban courier has overlapping downtown routes that make each new stop cheaper. A salesperson wants suburban accounts with larger invoices. What should guide the decision?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch06:q03: A university lab owns a rare instrument. Its real availability is weekend access because classes use it midweek. Which action protects power?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch06:q04: A regional insurer learns local storm damage patterns faster than national carriers because adjusters return clean notes every week. What would weaken this source of power?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch06:q05: A farm cooperative can chill berries within an hour, but a new buyer wants volume that would leave crates warm for three hours. What should the cooperative do?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch06:q06: A language school gets most lasting students from alumni referrals, but the team wants to spend its budget on a large ad campaign. Which question matters most?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch06:q07: A startup claims its power is a clever onboarding prank that customers loved once. Repeat cohorts show no improvement. What is the right diagnosis?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch06:q08: A company has a patented component, but service failures make customers avoid it. A competitor lacks the patent but has a trusted repair network. Which source is stronger?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch06:q09: A retailer copies a competitor’s store display but not the inventory system that keeps popular sizes in stock. What error is it making?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch07:q01: A warehouse safety team has ten injury categories, but hand cuts at one station cause most lost time. Which action best uses leverage?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch07:q02: A newspaper has a renewal problem. Expiring subscribers cluster on two late-delivery routes. What should renewal week prioritize?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch07:q03: A medtech sales team keeps adding demos after hospital reviews stall. Procurement records show one compliance packet is missing every time. What is the leveraged move?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch07:q04: A rail crew wants a full-line inspection, but one switch causes most rain delays. The rain window is short. What does leverage require?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch07:q05: A community bank plans a general fraud email. Alert data show new business checking accounts drive the largest losses. What mistake would the email make?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch07:q06: An online course platform loses users between signup and the first lesson. The team wants badges, community features, and pricing tests. What should come first?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch07:q07: A manager says leverage means making every process 10 percent more efficient. What is missing?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch07:q08: A nonprofit focuses all energy on one donor segment because it is easiest to reach. Results do not change because that segment was never the funding bottleneck. How should you judge the move?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch07:q09: A city road team can fix one intersection before school starts. Crash data show one crossing causes most injuries, but council members want small fixes in every district. What should guide the decision?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch08:q01: A school wants to transform attendance over five years, but records show ninth graders miss Mondays after bus pass renewals. What makes a good proximate objective?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch08:q02: A cybersecurity team says it will modernize everything, but payroll is exposed and has a patch window next week. What should come first?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch08:q03: A restaurant group wants to reinvent lunch, but line data show the cold sandwich lane falls behind before noon. Which objective is proximate?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch08:q04: A public health unit wants district-wide vaccination gains. A dose shipment conflicts with one school testing day at one clinic. What objective guides action best?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch08:q05: An architecture firm has a full campus vision, but permit comments focus on stormwater and access for one building. What is the strategic value of a prototype?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch08:q06: A sports club wants promotion but has three weak opponents next. Training is scattered across fitness, tactics, morale, and recruitment. What should the coach do?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch08:q07: A manager calls a target proximate because it is easy: archive old files by Friday. The actual obstacle is delayed customer onboarding. What is wrong?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch08:q08: A team refuses to set a near target because it cannot see the full path. It keeps discussing the ultimate goal. How should you evaluate this?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch08:q09: A nonprofit wants to end youth homelessness. Its next constraint is getting ten shelter beds staffed for winter nights. Which target is most proximate?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch09:q01: A surgical unit improves sterilizer speed, but cases still fail because clean trays go to the wrong room. What does chain-link thinking require?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch09:q02: An ecommerce returns team wants new label printers, but refunds wait two days at inspection. What should be fixed first?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch09:q03: A concert venue has fast ticket scanners and polite ushers, yet lines fail because oversized bags stop entry. What is the compensation error?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch09:q04: A solar installer adds crews while projects wait in a municipal permit portal. What is likely to happen?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch09:q05: A hotel breakfast manager buys better pastries after complaints, but guests still wait with no clean plates. What should a strategist see?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch09:q06: A university admissions office improves its application portal, but decisions remain late because transcripts wait in verification. What is the system cap?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch09:q07: A manager says every part of a process should improve by 5 percent. One required approval step fails half the time. What is wrong with the approach?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch09:q08: A team labels every weakness a chain link and chases all of them at once. Which test should sort them?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch09:q09: A software onboarding flow has beautiful emails and fast account creation, but identity verification fails for 30 percent of users. What action fits chain-link logic?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch10:q01: An outdoor gear brand improves its store display but keeps repair and warranty separate. Customers still doubt durability. Which design move fits the strategy?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch10:q02: A transit app uses one route name, bus stop signs use another, and fare cards use a third. What should the team do first?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch10:q03: A telehealth clinic improves its intake form, triage script, and follow-up text separately. Patients still fall through. What is missing?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch10:q04: A farmers market wants better customer flow. The token box sits after the busiest stall, so shoppers pass it before they can buy. What is the design response?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch10:q05: An enterprise software company charges extra for guided setup, but accounts without setup never reach usage levels that support expansion. Which choice shows design thinking?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch10:q06: A bike-share program places docks by district, repairs by complaint volume, and surveys by marketing interest. Commuters still find broken bikes. What is the flaw?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch10:q07: A leader says a strategy is well designed because the document is clean and visually consistent. What should you ask?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch10:q08: A competitor copies one visible part of a designed system, but not the supporting choices around it. Why may the copy fail?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch10:q09: A school improves tutoring, parent texts, and bus coordination separately. Attendance does not move because each team uses different student lists. What design fix matters?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch11:q01: A boutique law firm markets four practice areas, but wage-theft hearings create the fastest wins and referrals. What does strategic focus require?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch11:q02: A bakery wants both a wide retail spread and reliable wholesale morning delivery. The same ovens serve both. What should it do?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch11:q03: A career office runs popular general events, but first-generation students miss placement support before interviews. What is the focused move?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch11:q04: An industrial supplier can serve many segments, but food-processing shutdowns create the most urgent demand. What does focus change?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch11:q05: A music festival responds to sound complaints by adding more genres and stages. What is the likely strategic problem?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch11:q06: A mental health nonprofit has volunteers spread across workshops, newsletters, peer groups, and discharge calls. Data show the first forty-eight hours after discharge carry the highest risk. What should lead?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch11:q07: A team says it is focused because it has fewer slides and shorter meetings, but every priority still receives equal resources. What is missing?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch11:q08: A company stays focused on one segment even after that segment stops rewarding its effort. What is the best evaluation?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch11:q09: A public agency claims it cannot focus because all services matter. One service controls most legal risk and citizen harm this quarter. What should happen?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch12:q01: A fitness chain wants a third studio, but the coach roster shows the best coaches already carry retention classes. What is the right growth test?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch12:q02: A meal-kit company can add two cities, but cold-chain tests fail in one route pattern. What should it do?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch12:q03: A trade school opens a satellite before employer placements exist nearby. Enrollment rises but apprenticeships fall. What did growth weaken?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch12:q04: An accounting firm wants advisory growth during audit season, using the same senior partners who protect audit quality. What should leaders ask?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch12:q05: A clinic network signs a cheap lease outside its referral-dense area. Specialist schedules become thin and waits grow. How should this be judged?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch12:q06: A children’s publisher receives a broad foreign rights offer, but translation samples weaken the early-reader pacing. What is the strategic response?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch12:q07: A founder says revenue growth proves the strategy is working. Costs show the new customers require custom support that pulls engineers from the core product. What is the flaw?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch12:q08: A focused business rejects every adjacent opportunity for years, even ones that use the same capability and customers ask for. What risk appears?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch12:q09: A logistics firm adds regions faster than dispatcher training can support. Customer reliability falls. What should guide the next decision?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch13:q01: A retrofit contractor can book every rebate job this month, but only some jobs will certify crews for the next wave. Which choice best uses dynamics?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch13:q02: A resale marketplace is deciding whether to discount buyer prices in October or guarantee high-quality sellers earlier in September. The seller calendar shows the best inventory leaves before cold weather. What should the team do?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch13:q03: A port authority lost a carrier because dredging approval came after the carrier's commitment deadline. Leaders want a new marketing push. Which diagnosis fits the dynamics test?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch13:q04: A mobile game team wants to release its whole asset backlog before a competitor launch. The retention graph shows players drop after day seven. Which plan best reads dynamics?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch13:q05: A grocery delivery service wants to widen its zone fence, but the density heat map shows two strong neighborhoods and costly scattered routes elsewhere. What is the dynamic move?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch13:q06: An apprenticeship nonprofit sees employer demand shifting, but the cohort list is already nearly full. Which action uses timing and reaction instead of static planning?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch13:q07: A software company says it is using dynamics because it holds daily meetings and changes priorities whenever a competitor announces something. What is the weakness in that claim?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch13:q08: A museum can launch a membership drive now or first secure three local school partnerships that would bring families into the building all spring. Which evaluation is strongest?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch13:q09: A clinic network has one lease available now, but patient referrals are moving toward telehealth follow-ups. Leaders want to sign quickly before the landlord moves on. What should they examine first?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch14:q01: A legacy insurer keeps missing quote targets after a new script is introduced. The admin screen still requires four obsolete fields before a quote can move. What is the best diagnosis?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch14:q02: A hospital sees patient complaints cluster around shift changes. Leaders want a service-quality campaign, but the handoff log loses key details. What should they do first?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch14:q03: A university department cannot add modern courses because the catalog sequence depends on professors who retired years ago. Which action best counters inertia?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch14:q04: A plant has three versions of a shift standard near the same machine, and scrap is rising. Supervisors want a stricter discipline memo. What would address entropy?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch14:q05: A broadcaster says producers resist digital change. The editing queue still gives broadcast deadlines first claim on every editor, so online clips arrive late. What is the strongest move?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch14:q06: A food bank network finds spoiled produce every Friday. Volunteer texts, pickup schedules, and expiry labels are out of sequence. Which response fits the strategic move?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch14:q07: A manager says, "People just hate change," after a software rollout fails. Logs show the old tool remains faster for common tasks. What should you challenge?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch14:q08: A city agency has five pilot programs that started strong but now use different intake forms, metrics, and handoffs. Leaders want a sixth pilot. What is the better evaluation?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch14:q09: A sales team misses follow-ups because the CRM, calendar, and renewal spreadsheet disagree. The director wants a motivational contest. What should happen first?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch15:q01: An airport task force has runway phasing, noise complaints, and bond timing in separate files. What does synthesis require?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch15:q02: A district has poor attendance in two neighborhoods, driver vacancies, and route failures from the same depot. Which plan best puts the pieces together?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch15:q03: A medical device team has broad sales ambitions, cautious regulatory guidance, and strongest evidence in one hospital segment. What is the integrated move?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch15:q04: A tourism board wants to recover from a weak season with six events, a brand campaign, and hotel discounts. Data shows midweek shoulder-season rooms are the actual gap. What should leaders do?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch15:q05: A security program lists dozens of risks, but the architecture diagram shows one identity service touching critical systems. What action best reflects synthesis?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch15:q06: A water utility ranks projects by pipe age, but crew windows, permit timing, and funding hearings point to a different order. Which response is strongest?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch15:q07: A nonprofit strategy document has sections on diagnosis, policy, actions, timing, and measures, but the measures track goals unrelated to the diagnosis. What is the flaw?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch15:q08: A regional clinic plan includes a staffing fix, a scheduling change, and a patient education push. Which evidence would best show the pieces are truly integrated?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch15:q09: A product team says it has put everything together because its roadmap includes customer research, engineering capacity, and launch dates. What should you test?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch16:q01: A funding request asks for a brand campaign, but churn data points to service delays. What makes the request strategically rigorous?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch16:q02: A reform team says intake outreach will reduce missed appointments, but service data shows people drop out during document review. What should happen?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch16:q03: An investment memo argues a company has pricing power, but the bear case shows margins fall whenever large buyers renegotiate. What should the committee require?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch16:q04: A product team wants to run a pricing test called "prove willingness to pay," but the card names no buyer or behavior. What is the best next step?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch16:q05: A lab wants equipment funding, but a failed replication note questions the effect the equipment would study. What is the disciplined move?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch16:q06: A hospital dashboard shows average wait time improving, but severe incidents cluster after specialist consults. Which board decision is most rigorous?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch16:q07: A startup strategy says, "Customers will love the new platform because it is modern." What is the main scientific weakness?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch16:q08: A city transport plan predicts that bus shelters will increase ridership, but early data shows ridership rises only on routes with schedule reliability fixes. What should leaders conclude?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch16:q09: A leadership team says its strategy is scientific because it includes a spreadsheet model, but no one can say what result would change the plan. What is missing?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch17:q01: A founder wants to copy a rival's freemium pivot, but customer interviews show her buyers need trust before trial. What should she do?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch17:q02: A campaign team has a clean story about transit voters, but cross-tabs show the message works only when paired with school pickup times. What is the disciplined move?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch17:q03: A principal assumes families do not value attendance routines, but teacher notes and parent calls point to bus transfers and late work shifts. What should change?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch17:q04: A supply-chain director receives a port delay alert and wants to pay for air freight on every part. Supplier emails show only one component threatens assembly. What is the best move?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch17:q05: A consultant compares a client to a fast-growing peer, but client facts show different margins, contracts, and staffing rules. What should she do?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch17:q06: A grant committee loves one applicant after a vivid site visit, but the outcome table is thin and the rubric rewards measurable results. What is the disciplined sequence?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch17:q07: A leader says, "This is just like the last turnaround," and the team relaxes. The market, cost structure, and customer trust are all different. What is the risk?

good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch17:q08: A nonprofit director prefers evidence showing a beloved program works, but neutral data suggests another program has stronger outcomes. Which response best shows active judgment?
good-strategy-bad-strategy-ch17:q09: A manager wants to act fast because the first explanation feels obvious. What quick check would most improve the decision?
